clauses.reason: The sentence exempts Arthur A. Quinn from compulsory retirement for age “for an indefinite period of time, not extending beyond June 30, 1951”. The order fixes no earlier end event, so the stated date is the latest date the exemption could last and is the best supported end date. It is recorded inclusive (through June 30, 1951); the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins. An earlier lapse, such as separation from office, is not shown by any held source and is disclosed as unestablished.

inventory_overrides.reason: Corrected inventory: the operative sentence as one clause, replacing the dossier's fragment ending at the words 'not extending beyond June 30,' and the separate fragment '1951.'

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10215 (16 FR 1703 (Federal Register of February 20, 1951)) was signed February 16, 1951. Its held Federal Register text prints the order number, the title and the signing date. Its only operative command exempts Arthur A. Quinn, Comptroller of Customs with headquarters at New York, New York, from compulsory retirement for age under the Civil Service Retirement Act of May 29, 1930, as amended, under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932, “for an indefinite period of time, not extending beyond June 30, 1951”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated: by its own words the exemption cannot extend beyond June 30, 1951. The period is described as indefinite but capped, so the cap is the latest date on which the exemption could be in force. No held source shows that the exemption lapsed earlier (for example by Mr. Quinn's separation from office), and none shows any extension: the person-name search of the held order texts found no other order naming him, and the held-text search for the order's number found no citation. The Federal Register disposition-note, U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit naming this order. The best supported date is therefore June 30, 1951, recorded on the inclusive reading, with the possibility of an earlier factual lapse disclosed. The dossier split the sentence into a long fragment and the five-character fragment “1951.”; the inventory is corrected to the single operative sentence.
